claims.text: A multiscale physics-informed machine-learning surrogate using hierarchical microstructural descriptors can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior.
The surrogate will require roughly one-tenth of the computation time of full-scale DFT and finite-element simulations.
The surrogate will predict the target mechanical properties within ±10% of experimental measurements.
The reported HfNbTiVAl10 has a deliberately engineered hierarchical heterostructure containing controlled nanoscale precipitates and phase boundaries.
Nanoscale precipitates and phase boundaries in HfNbTiVAl10 affect dislocation mobility.
Nanoscale precipitates and phase boundaries in HfNbTiVAl10 affect crack propagation.
Misfit volumes, elastic constants, and phase-fraction data are relevant model inputs for predicting mechanical behavior.
Imaging- and spectroscopy-derived microstructural descriptors can be integrated with computed parameters in the proposed surrogate.
The hierarchical heterostructure mediates local stress fields.
Hierarchical intragranular nanoprecipitates enhance dislocation accumulation or storage.
Nanoscale precipitates reinforce the matrix.
Phase boundaries deflect crack propagation.
The surrogate captures contributions from solid-solution strengthening, heterostructure-induced toughening, and interfacial barrier effects.
Representing those mechanisms in a reduced-order framework bypasses the computational demands of DFT/FEM while retaining essential microstructural information.
The surrogate will predict crack-initiation and propagation pathways consistent with in situ fracture observations.
Full-scale DFT combined with finite-element simulation is computationally intensive for this prediction task.
Conventional simulations may not fully capture hierarchical microstructural effects.
The surrogate may fail when defects, phase instabilities, or anisotropies lie outside its input or calibration range.
The surrogate may fail when effective-medium approximations neglect important scale-dependent phenomena.
Young’s modulus can be measured from the initial elastic slope of a tensile stress-strain curve.
